title: Common Ancestors for Many Pairs of Nodes

concept.title: Lift the deeper node to the same depth, then lift both as high as possible while they differ
body: The *lowest common ancestor* (LCA) of two nodes is the deepest node that is an ancestor of both (a node is its own ancestor). Walking up one step at a time, as in the simple solution, costs O(depth) per query; for many queries on a tall tree use the table of the previous task, `up[j][v]` = the 2^j-th ancestor of `v` (0 if none).

1. **Equalize the depths.** If `u` is deeper than `v` by `diff`, lift `u` by `diff` steps using the bits of `diff`. If now `u == v`, that node is the answer.
2. **Lift both together.** Go through `j` from the highest bit to 0. If the ancestors `up[j][u]` and `up[j][v]` are **different**, jump both (they are still below the LCA). In the end `u` and `v` are different children of the LCA, so the answer is their parent `up[0][u]`.

The depths come from a breadth-first walk from the root (the parents of this task can have larger numbers than their children, so the node numbers give no order). A query costs O(log n), and the table O(n log n). No recursion is used anywhere, so a path of 20000 nodes is no problem.

statement: A tree with `n` nodes is given by the parent of each node (0 for the root). For each query `u v`, print the lowest common ancestor of the nodes `u` and `v`: the deepest node that has both of them in its subtree (a node is in its own subtree).
inputFormat: The first line has `n`, the number of nodes (numbered 1 to n).
The second line has `n` numbers: for each node its parent, and 0 for the root.
The third line has `q`, the number of queries.
Each of the next `q` lines has two nodes `u` and `v`.
outputFormat: `q` lines: the lowest common ancestor of every pair.
constraints: The numbers describe one tree: exactly one node has the parent 0, and following parents always reaches it.
A parent can have a larger number than its child.
The tree can be a long path (depth up to n - 1).

examples.note: The nodes 4 and 5 are the children of 2; 4 and 6 meet at the root 1; the node 2 is an ancestor of 4.

hints: Compute the depth of every node with a breadth-first walk and build the table up[j][v].
First lift the deeper node so both have the same depth; if they are equal now, that is the answer.
Then, for j from the highest bit down, jump both nodes when their 2^j-th ancestors differ; the answer is the parent.

solution.complexity: Time O(n log n + q log n), space O(n log n).
